title: Packing House Coffee
text:
Met with Steve Paulette and Sally.
Nicole: Highlighted point for local leaders to make connections at provincial and federal level to open up lines of communication to enact change. Cache Creek Packing House owner Steve was former local government official who made connection at provincial level so that he could have important meetings allowing things such as road development and fishing restrictions could be passed.
Trish: I keep coming back to the notion of consultation - if you ask those who are local, they will work with you and help you. Example, if they had consulted, they could have prevented the decimation of the trout population at Steelhead.

title: Wildfires
text: The challenges faced are real and urgent, climate change being one of the largest. We heard a lot about wildfires during our trip and saw the devastation that they can cause. After we returned home, Jasper, where we had been staying was ravaged by fire and we witnessed shocking pictures of the town in ashes.

title: Bernie and Lorna from Kumsheen Rafting
text:
They started their business 50 years (to the day) before we arrived!
Adele: Entrepreneurship is hard work - with or without employees. Remain focused on vision. Start small than expand. Listen to all stakeholders but must develop the ability to know whom to listen too.
Su: When no one has heard of river rafting and even question the sustainability of the business, they were firm believers of their own passion, overcoming obstacles and eventually build up the adventure tourism in Lytton and go on to create awareness on the importance of river ecology and the effect of climate change on Thomson River. And when the wild forest fire engulfed Lytton they immediately begin rebuilding, knowing many families depend on Kumsheen to put food on their tables.
Trish: Having a community helps people get through the difficult times - theater, art, music programs provide a place to gather, be together, be involved
Nicole: Community focused business can still be profitable and provide a great place to work. Kumsheen rafting is a family owned for-profit business which caters to the need of the community. Bank burned down = Scotiabank temporary bank on property. Forestry worker housing burnt down = open up space on property. Company pushing government to take action by staying involved and holding inaction accountable.

title: Fairmont Hotel
text:
At the Fairmont Hotel Claire and Shane from their team we met talked about the concept of servant leadership. Nicole: They described it as an "upside down pyramid style leadership. The "management level" are at the bottom to provide support to the front line staff who provide the guest experience and do the important work. Their job is to remove obstacles preventing staff from reaching their objectives."
An article explaining the concept.

title: Greg Stewart, President of the Sinclair Group
text:
Greg is a third-generation leader of Sinclar. He talked about a lot of interesting topics, including how Sinclair tries to be environmentally concious (3 trees planted for every one taken, removing dead lumber can help increase the health of the forest and reduce wildfire risk, excess heat from the Mill is used to warm municipal buildings), how they work with First Nations and how they incorporated AI into their processes.
Nicole: While becoming more efficient for operations, more jobs in the tech side are created as opposed to traditional jobs on the maintenance side. From a labour standpoint, agreed with the method of a hiring freeze when AI was introduced and not re-filling now redundant positions.

title: Dinner in Jasper
text:
Muhammed: During the dinner with Todd, Greg the Fire Chief,/a> and other Jasper community leaders, we gained valuable insights into forest wildfire management (from Landon Shepherd, a fire and vegetation specialist with Parks Canada) and the importance of community engagement. Todd's team's dedication and commitment to protecting the wilderness while actively involving the local community were truly inspiring. Their stories reminded us of the power of collaboration and the positive impact it can have on both nature and society after making Jasper home 25-30 years ago.
Additionally, I was captivated by those who came to Jasper for holidays and ended up staying indefinitely. This exemplified the profound effect that a place like Jasper can have on people, drawing them in with its charm and creating a deep sense of belonging
Kai: Not enough is being done in Jasper to drive diversity, opportunities, change. Pale male and stale

title: Heating in Prince George
text: We met the Mayor of Prince George, Simon Yu who has had a fascinating journey from his birthplace in Hong Kong. He showed us the heating facility that uses the waste heat from the sawmill kiln, itself powered by waste sawdust, to heat 13 of the government buildings in their community. The tangible success of this pilot is being used to inspire and drive expansion. He also gave us some Prince George branded socks with the town's slightly terrifying mascot on them.

title: Mike and Cheryl's Drum Circle in Barkerville
text: The drum circle in Barkerville was a wonderful experience. When we did the first one, I loved to learn that it orginally evolved as a practical way to scare off bears (Many community building traditions we encountered had practical roots), but after hearing Mike and Sheryl's emotional stories about the hardships their community had faced in previous generations and their own the final drum circle we did before we left took on a deeper emotional signifcance.

title: Bus Breakdown
text:
On the way to the glacier, the bus broke down because it was overheating. It was lovely how many people stopped and offered to help, including one guy in an interestingly decorated car with a doll strapped to the hood. We made it to a rest area and there we managed to get a lift with a lovely tour bus of Germans who took us to the Glacier and Skywalk.
Kali: Resilience and adaptability are sure signs of a great leader and are valuable in every facet of life. We had a testing journey that would have broken many teams apart, however we had fun, trusted the process and each other, and took all the challenges as they came. Regardless of the drama, I had the best day yesterday! Also, when you need to hitchhike and catch a random bus with strangers, call Ed :)
Caroline: The best decision for a team (or organization) isn’t always the perfect decision. Some sacrifices have to be made and some risks taken in order to reap some (or more) benefits. Like leaving our luggage behind! I know not everyone was comfortable with it and some even thought it was a bad idea. At that point our options were: A) status quo or B) take a leap of faith. I imagine that the rest of the day would have turned out very different had we not taken that leap of faith to leave our luggage behind.

title: Spirit Island at Maligne Lake
text: As we traveled along our journey, we met Dr. Rebekah Ingram, an expert at Carleton University on Indigenous languages, who said, when discussing the meaning and origins of Indigenous words, “The way that I had been thinking was based exclusively on the viewpoint of the world that I did not even know that I had; we were not being critical of our own information sources.”

title: Encampment in Prince George
text: Prince George had a large tent encampment of homeless people, a complex challenge caused by problems with housing affordability, addiction and other issues. This camp was actually closed down in 2025, under the condition that the 20 residents at the time were found suitable accomodation and didn't apply for an exemption.
